title: The Cow That Kept Giving Milk

beats.text: History's most famous bad day to buy stocks didn't cost you twenty-five years.
September third, nineteen twenty-nine. You're Walter, a Brooklyn tailor, buying at the very top.
The Dow closes at three hundred eighty-one. Then October hits.
By July nineteen thirty-two, it's forty-one. Eighty-nine percent, gone.
Your neighbors panic and sell. You just keep sewing.
The Dow won't see three eighty-one again until nineteen fifty-four.
So how are you back to even by nineteen thirty-six?
You see, a stock is a cow. Its price crashes at the fair, but it still gives milk.
At the bottom, dividends paid almost fourteen percent of the price, and you reinvest every check.
Meanwhile, everything gets cheaper. Living costs fall over eighteen percent.
Every dollar buys more bread, more cloth, more shares.
Count the milk and the cheaper bread, and you're even by late nineteen thirty-six.
The Dow took twenty-five years. The cow never stopped giving milk.

facts.claim: The Dow Jones Industrial Average peaked at 381.17 (close) on September 3, 1929
Black Monday Oct 28 and Black Tuesday Oct 29, 1929 (the crash came in October)
The Dow closed at 41.22 on July 8, 1932, 89 percent below its peak
The Dow did not regain its 1929 high until November 23, 1954 (about 25 years)
At the mid-1932 low the stock market's dividend yield was close to 14 percent (Shiller data)
The CPI in late 1936 was more than 18 percent lower than in fall 1929

Counting dividends and deflation, a lump-sum investor in the average stock at the 1929 high was back to break-even by late 1936 (about 7 years; Hulbert, NYT 2009). Fool.ca cites an even shorter real-terms figure; we use the conservative one.
Walter the Brooklyn tailor is a fictional everyman

caption:
Bought stocks at the very top in 1929? The Dow needed 25 years to get back to 381.
But dividends near 14% at the bottom and falling prices got investors back to even by late 1936.
